canberra.title: CIT to cut more executive staff in new restructure proposal
canberra.snippet: The Canberra Institute of Technology is pressing ahead with a proposed restructure amid two governance reviews, a voluntary redundancy pr...
canberra.content:
CIT is trying to get its house in order after years of uncertainty and tumult. Photo: Ian Bushnell.

The Canberra Institute of Technology is pressing ahead with a proposed restructure amid two governance reviews, a voluntary redundancy program and the University of Canberra seeking a merger.

The restructure proposal, which includes a further reduction in executive roles, was sent to staff members for consultation on Tuesday (10 November).

It aims to clarify accountability, strengthen governance, better align education and support functions, and aid the long-term financial sustainability of the troubled organisation.

In a move that will be well received by staff, the executive arm will be further downsized, with two roles no longer required going forward. Two positions were lost last year, meaning the executive will shrink from 13 to nine.

A CIT spokesperson said these decisions reflected organisational design and future operating requirements, not the value or contribution of the people involved.

CIT has long faced staff criticism that it was too top-heavy and needed to focus more on its teaching staff and reduce its executive, including the associated salary bill.

But with the restructure pursuing financial sustainability, the voluntary redundancy program announced in August will continue.

The Sustainable Workforce Program also included deferring new hires and not renewing contracts, and covered all permanent staff across the organisation.

The CIT spokesperson said the organisation was progressing the redesign of its organisational structure and a draft functional structure was shared with staff for consultation.

“These proposed changes include some reporting line and branch structure changes and consultation is open until COB Thursday 19 November,” the spokesperson said.

“All staff are encouraged to engage throughout the consultation process. Feedback from staff and unions will help inform final decisions.”

The CIT board could have been forgiven for holding back on a restructure amid all the other activity, but it must have believed it could not wait.

Board chair Tom Rogers indicated to Region in August, when CEO Dr Margot McNeill resigned, that the board wanted to draw a line under the episode and take the organisation forward.

Mr Rogers said the board was “right-sizing” the organisation in response to the top-heavy criticism and that CIT could not keep running up deficits like last year’s $28 million result and go cap in hand to government for top-ups.

The board was looking to shave 10 per cent off CIT’s annual operating budget.

“We’ve got to look at all areas of our operation, and in any public sector organisation, there’s stuff that can be done differently,” he said.

But he stressed this should not detract from student learning.

On the merger proposal, Mr Rogers said he was open to any arrangement that would help put the cash-strapped training organisation on a more sustainable path.

The ACT Government is conducting its own review of governance while a Legislative Assembly committee is also inquiring into CIT governance, including the proposed merger with UC.

UC Vice-Chancellor Bill Shorten has been marshalling support for the merger and last week spruiked the university’s submission to the committee inquiry, which maps out a path to a new dual-sector institution by 2029.

In recent years, CIT has endured a contracts scandal, a corruption finding and the appointment of a new CEO that went horribly wrong, revealing even more governance flaws and further damaging its reputation.

canberra.title: Could Canberrans be forced to update their Medicare info to recover lost millions in GST revenue?
canberra.snippet: The ACT Government is seriously considering forcing Canberrans to update their Medicare details if the Commonwealth doesn’t improve...
canberra.content:
10 November 2026

Start the conversation

When’s the last time you updated your Medicare details? Photo: John Lomnicki.

The ACT Government is seriously considering forcing Canberrans to update their Medicare details if the Commonwealth doesn’t improve how it calculates GST distribution.

It’s been a long-running saga that Canberra’s population is undercounted by the Australian Bureau of Statistics, which uses Medicare address information to forecast population growth.

This forecast is used between censuses to determine how much GST revenue is distributed across jurisdictions.

The ACT’s recent population variance was 5.2 per cent, resulting in the Territory losing out on $550 million in GST revenue.

That equated to about $4000 lost per person.

“The error of our population [count] has tripled in size every census for the past three censuses,” Treasury Economic and Financial acting executive group manager Chris Roberts told annual reports hearings.

The government submitted to the current Productivity Commission inquiry that this needed to be addressed. An interim report suggested the ACT encourage people to voluntarily update their Medicare addresses.

Treasurer Chris Steel told the annual reports hearings this had already been tried.

“I thought that was a pretty unusual comment to make,” he said.

Another suggestion has been to instead force Canberrans, particularly its younger, transient population, to update their Medicare addresses.

“We could, tomorrow, make the Medicare addresses the sole source of truth for someone’s residency in the ACT,” Mr Steel said.

“I don’t think we want to take that step – I haven’t ruled it out – but I think there’s a way of doing this that is less coercive.”

It has not been suggested that Canberrans would be prevented from accessing healthcare services unless their details were updated.

Instead, it would be aimed at government-storefront interactions, such as when someone applies to update their driver licence details, which is mandatory when you change addresses.

Mr Steel hoped any forced updating would come from the Commonwealth, but said the ACT Government had to consider its options if its Federal counterparts weren’t prepared to act.

“I don’t want to go down that path, because I don’t think it’s necessary when there could be a simple, true reconciliation process that could be established by the Commonwealth,” he said.

“We have to prepare for a situation where the Commonwealth is not prepared to act if things get worse – and it’s quite possible that they are.

“We can’t have a situation where we’re funding services for a population that we’re not receiving any revenue for.”

Another issue raised with the GST revenue process was the flow-on impact to other funding capabilities.

Mr Roberts pointed out that while the direct cost was recently $550 million, the flow-on impact was about twice that size.

“We have the largest percentage error in the population estimates,” he said.

Mr Steel implored people living in the ACT to update their Medicare details right away.

“You’ll be helping to contribute to the services that you use,” he said.

canberra.title: No charges against OpenAI for its data breach against Services Australia
canberra.snippet: The Federal Government has accepted all recommendations from the rapid review of OpenAI’s recent breach of Services Australia’s Medicare ...
canberra.content:
An OpenAI agent hacked Services Australia’s Medicare data in June but didn’t report it until September, and won’t face any legal charges. Photo: John Lomnicki.

The Federal Government has accepted all recommendations from the rapid review of OpenAI’s recent breach of Services Australia’s Medicare data, but criminal charges against the tech company are not among them.

Anthony Albanese accepted the review’s recommendations on Tuesday (10 November) without actually releasing the review itself, which he said would be distributed in due course.

“The clear indication is that no information was got that involves people’s personal details. All of that was confirmed essentially,” the Prime Minister said.

“The implications of this, in fact, were minor in terms of direct implications.

“But that doesn’t mean that it wasn’t a serious issue and that in other areas there might be more serious implications.”

The PM suggested changes to Australia’s criminal law would be made to get tough on future breaches by artificial intelligence companies.

He said work was already underway on implementing the review’s 18 recommendations.

“We accept all of the recommendations, and we have commenced work to implement them,” Mr Albanese said.

“AI offers Australia and the world generational opportunities if we seize and shape them properly, and that is exactly what we are doing here.”

The Prime Minister also announced mandatory AI rules that will be included in Labor’s AI legislation, and that will be regulated by a new AI safety regulator with teeth.

“One of the first things that we are doing here today is announcing our mandatory AI Safety and Security Protections, which will be part of our AI legislation,” he said.

“As part of that, these protections will be regulated by a new targeted AI safety regulator who will be able to enforce significant penalties for AI companies doing the wrong thing.”

The Prime Minister said six main areas of attention align with the recommendations from the Parliamentary Joint Select Committee on Artificial Intelligence.

They include requiring AI companies to maintain security controls across all stages of development and deployment; identify and manage serious risks associated with their models; and provide mandatory, rapid incident notifications to the Australian Government.

They will also have to allow independent evaluation of their models; maintain and publish safety and security frameworks to ensure good governance and transparency; and update standards and rules as technologies change.

A key recommendation of the rapid review is for the Attorney-General’s Department, the Australian Federal Police and the Home Affairs Department to consider reforming the law to introduce “penalties for egregious regulatory non-compliance” by AI companies.

Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said the government needed to make sure “our laws and our systems keep pace with the technology”.

He said it was also necessary to use the technology to find vulnerabilities before others do.

“The mandatory reporting, when artificial intelligence goes rogue, gives us a chance to be able to make sure that when this happens, the reporting occurs and occurs immediately,” Mr Burke said.

“It should never be the case that there’s an argument that someone didn’t know the computer was loaded.

“We need to make sure that the criminal law is up to date for how this new technology is able to act.”

An OpenAI agent gained unauthorised access to the Medicare statistics reporting service portal administered in June, but did not inform the Federal Government of the breach until September.

Greens leader David Shoebridge described the government’s announcement on Tuesday of a new AI regulator as a “toothless tiger” and a “predictable capitulation to the interests of vampire US tech corporations” over Australian people.

“The Prime Minister had the gall to announce another regulator without the powers and protections needed to hold these corporations to account,” Senator Shoebridge said.

“It’s utterly bizarre that just weeks after OpenAI was implicated in hacking a Medicare portal, the government’s key recommendation is to get closer to OpenAI.

“Sending public servants on secondment to the companies they’re meant to regulate is how regulators get captured. When those companies are vampire US AI companies, the risks of this strategy are obvious.

“The weak recommendations in this review fall well short of responding to the real and growing public concern; a case in point is that even OpenAI supports mandatory reporting, while the PM only promises to ‘consider’ it.”

The Coalition welcomed the announcement, saying it was pleased the government had adopted a number of the initial recommendations of the multipartisan Parliamentary Joint Select Committee on Artificial Intelligence.

Shadow home affairs minister Jonno Duniam said the Opposition will continue to engage constructively with the government and the committee as the work progresses.

“Artificial intelligence has massive potential to transform Australia for the better, but politicians need to ensure that new technologies are developed and deployed safely and responsibly,” Senator Duniam said.

canberra.title: Qantas to slash 850 back office jobs as part of offshoring and AI partnership
canberra.snippet: Qantas has announced its intention to slash 850 jobs over the next few years as it converts some administration roles to be performed by ...
canberra.content:
Qantas will cut about 850 jobs as they are offshored or converted to artificial intelligence agents. Photo: Andrew McLaughlin.

Qantas has announced its intention to slash 850 jobs over the next few years as it converts some administration roles to be performed by artificial intelligence, and offshores others.

The announcement coincides with the airline signing a strategic partnership with AI giant Accenture “to modernise its back-end systems, processes and data, as it steps up investment in technology and AI”.

The airline says it is responding to the pace of change in technology and AI globally, which it says is rapidly transforming how businesses operate, what customers expect and how people do their jobs.

“Like every airline, Qantas runs on technology built up over decades for a different era, including more than 1000 legacy applications that were never designed to work together,” a company statement reads.

“Modernising these systems and connecting the data across them is the critical next step to remove complexity, unlock innovation and accelerate the group’s use of AI, with lasting benefits across the business.”

The airline says the partnership with Accenture will redesign and simplify how parts of the company’s corporate functions operate. “Some of the services they provide will move to Accenture, delivered mostly by its teams in India and some in Australia, and in time be transformed further with automation and AI,” it says.

As a result, the airline – which touts itself as ‘the Spirit of Australia’ – says about 850 roles across the Qantas Group will be “affected over the coming years”. It says it will consult with affected employees and their unions before individual outcomes are determined, and that the first “wave of changes” are expected to be in place by mid-2027.

Qantas Group CEO Vanessa Hudson said the partnership with Accenture was about building a more modern, competitive organisation, and preparing the business for the future.

“The scale and speed of change in this space is unprecedented and unlike anything businesses have seen in generations,” she said.

“Leading organisations around the world are well progressed in using technology and AI to completely transform how they work, and standing still is not an option for us.

“We need to reinvent the processes, platforms and data behind our business so we can innovate faster and deliver a better, more connected experience for our customers and our people,” she added.

“That means fundamentally redesigning how the work behind our airline gets done, so it is simpler, more connected and keeps getting better, with automation and AI built in from the start.”

The announcement come less than a week after the airline revealed it is experiencing trading conditions in line with the outlook it provided for the financial year, despite a spike in fuel costs since June. It says demand continues to remain “resilient as customers continue to prioritise travel”, and that international and domestic leisure travel remains strong.

At the time of writing, the airline’s share price had risen 4.73 per cent to $9.75 on this morning’s announcement, but remains below its most recent high of $10.69 back in early August.

The Australian Services Union which represents much of the airline’s admin workforce said Qantas was using the “same old playbook” by blaming the cuts on AI.

It says the job cuts will mainly affect the airline’s Sydney workforce working in back office jobs including finance, people, procurement and marketing, with many of the roles expected to be transferred to India.

ASU NSW & ACT Secretary Angus McFarland said the announcement was devastating for Australian workers, and said it provided evidence that Qantas’ culture hadn’t changed under its new leadership.

“CEO Vanessa Hudson promised Australians a different Qantas,” he said.

“Instead she’s reaching straight for Alan Joyce’s old blueprint to cut Australian jobs, outsource them or send the work overseas and dress it all up as progress.

“Qantas wants us to believe this is about artificial intelligence and the future of aviation. But there’s really nothing innovative about shipping Australian jobs overseas to cut costs.”

The union said Qantas’ own communication to employees exposed contradictions. In an FAQ to employees, the airline reportedly confirmed the work would move predominantly to India, and that there would be no new AI systems or AI agents introduced on day one.

“Qantas talks endlessly about AI, but its own documents make it clear that the first step is to send Australian work to India,” Mr McFarland said.

“Technology should be used to make jobs better, not to provide another excuse to get rid of the people doing the hard work.

“This is a gut-wrenching blow to workers,” he added.

“These are skilled, experienced workers who have helped build one of Australia’s most recognisable companies. They make sure workers are safe and paid correctly, and do the jobs behind the scenes that keep the flying kangaroo running.

He said today’s announcement was particularly galling given what he says is the airline’s “awful history of outsourcing Australian jobs”.

“Qantas illegally and shamefully outsourced 1700 ground-handling workers under Alan Joyce,” he said.

“We were told Vanessa Hudson would lead a new chapter, but here we are again, watching Qantas betraying Australian workers by looking for another way to get them off their books.”

Original Article published by Andrew McLaughlin on PS News.

canberra.title: Grandfather accused of abusing his two young granddaughters
canberra.snippet: CONTENT WARNING: This article refers to alleged child abuse. A man from northern NSW has been allowed to drive back home after he was cha...
canberra.content:
10 November 2026

A 58-year-old man has been accused of indecently abusing his two granddaughters. Photo: Michelle Kroll.

CONTENT WARNING: This article refers to alleged child abuse.

A man from northern NSW has been allowed to drive back home after he was charged with indecently abusing his two young granddaughters in Canberra.

An ACT Policing spokesperson alleged the 58-year-old man, who cannot be named to protect the girls’ identities, committed multiple indecent acts against the children during separate incidents between January and September 2026.

The police spokesperson said the allegations were reported to their officers last weekend and the man was arrested the following day.

On Tuesday (10 November), the ACT Magistrates Court heard he was accused of indecently abusing his four-year-old granddaughter in January, then also indecently abusing his 11-year-old granddaughter in both June and September.

The court heard prosecutors did not oppose him being granted bail, but wanted a $1000 surety put in place to ensure he would return to court.

His lawyer, Legal Aid’s Eimear Silk, said he could provide a surety, but police had seized his phone, which he needed to transfer money between accounts to do so.

She also said his motorcycle was still parked outside his granddaughters’ house and asked that he be allowed to return once to collect it so he could ride to his home in northern NSW.

“I understand [he] is highly motivated to return to court to dispute the allegations,” Ms Silk said.

Special Magistrate Michael Cowen granted bail, but said he wouldn’t impose the surety as he didn’t think $1000 would incentivise anyone to return to court.

The prosecutor said she requested that amount because she understood the man received Centrelink benefits.

The man’s bail conditions include him living in northern NSW, not entering the ACT except for legal purposes and not approaching or contacting his granddaughters or their family. He was allowed to return to their home once to collect his motorcycle.

“You’re not to wave at them when you collect your motorbike, you understand that?” Special Magistrate Cowen told him.

The man has been charged with two counts of committing an act of indecency on a person under 16 and one count of committing an act of indecency on a person under 10.

No pleas were entered, and the matter was adjourned to December.

If this story has raised any concerns for you, 1800RESPECT, the national 24-hour sexual assault, family and domestic violence counselling line, can be contacted on 1800 737 732. Help and support are also available through the Canberra Rape Crisis Centre on 6247 2525, the Domestic Violence Crisis Service ACT on 6280 0900, the Sexual Violence Legal Services on 6257 4377 and Lifeline on 13 11 14. In an emergency, call triple zero.

If you have been affected by sexual violence, or someone you know has, you can report it to police by attending a police station or phoning 131 444.

australia.title: Victorian Labor’s ‘unforgivable’ preferences decision risks Liberal-One Nation government, Greens warn
australia.snippet: Exclusive: Ellen Sandell says Labor’s decision not to back progressives in key inner-seat could hand power to right-wing coalition in clo...
australia.content:
The Victorian Greens say Labor’s “frankly unforgivable” decision not to preference the minor party in a key inner-city seat could hand the upcoming election to a Liberal-One Nation coalition.

The party’s leader, Ellen Sandell, lambasted Labor’s decision on Tuesday to run an open ticket in Prahran, an inner Melbourne seat currently held by the Liberals’ Rachel Westaway on a tiny 1.3% margin.

It means Labor’s how-to-vote material will encourage voters to place their candidate, Meghan Hopper, first on the ballot but will not direct them how to allocate their remaining preferences. Instead, the remaining boxes on its how-to-vote material will probably remain blank.

Labor preferences are key to the Greens cinching back the seat, which they lost in a 2025 byelection.

The Greens received a 13.4% swing at the poll, with the result influenced by several factors, including Labor’s decision not to field a candidate, low voter turnout, a well-resourced campaign urging voters to put them last and unfavourable preference flows from other candidates. This included the former Labor MP Tony Lupton, who contested the byelection as an independent.

Sandell told Guardian Australia Labor was “showing its true colours” by running an open ticket, as it could inadvertently help the Liberals and One Nation not only secure the seat but also government.

“After months of scaremongering about a Liberal-One Nation government, Labor is now using its preferences to help elect one,” she said.

“This could be one of the most consequential elections in the state’s history. The result may come down to a single seat, and a divisive party like One Nation could hold the balance of power.

“It is frankly unforgivable that Labor would do a dodgy back-room deal to help elect a Liberal-One Nation government – and it’s something that Victorian voters will not easily forget.”

Sandell said Labor voters would be also “shocked” to see the party refusing to preference a “local, progressive Greens woman in Prahran”, Angelica Di Camillo, who also ran at the byelection.

Labor is also running an open ticket in the neighbouring seat of Caulfield, held by the Liberals’ David Southwick on a 2.1% margin. But it is expected Southwick will see a swing in his favour and comfortably retain the seat.

It is understood the local campaigns in Prahran and Caulfield requested the open ticket arrangement, which is consistent with the position Labor took at the 2025 federal election in the overlapping seat of Macnamara, held by Josh Burns, amid the height of the Israel-Hamas war in Gaza.

A Labor spokesperson said: “Our message is simple: put a 1 next to Labor candidates everywhere. We’re fighting for majority government.”

Caulfield is home to Victoria’s largest Jewish community, which also extends into St Kilda East in the Prahran electorate.

On Tuesday, the Liberals and Nationals also confirmed they would exchange preferences with One Nation, with the opposition leader, Jess Wilson, telling reporters how-to-vote cards for Coalition candidates would instruct voters to put Labor, the Greens and the Victorian Socialists “at the bottom of the ticket, and all other parties above that”.

Just hours after Wilson confirmed the position, One Nation moved to disendorse its Preston candidate, Franco Guardiani, over tweets, including one that described Hitler as the “GOAT”, an acronym which stands for greatest of all time.

The Victorian Liberal Senator Jane Hume told ABC’s Afternoon Briefing Guardiani’s tweets were “vile” and confirmed he would be last on the party’s how-to-vote material in the electorate.

australia.title: ‘How is this considered safe?’ Band-Aids no fix for Victoria’s ‘broken’ health system, doctors warn
australia.snippet: Ahead of the Victorian state election, medical professionals say patients’ care is being compromised by overwork and understaffing at hos...
australia.content:
Despite its challenges, Sarah* loves her job. After a decade working as a doctor, “it still feels like a privilege to do the work I do,” she says. “I do a lot of long hours and unpaid work, and generally accept this as going with the territory.”

While pregnant, Sarah worked night shifts until she was 30 weeks along, and then at 35 weeks worked 10 days in a row, including a 15-hour shift. “I would have worked 120 hours in the fortnight and not got paid overtime.”

The Victorian doctor, who has young children, is one of thousands of medical professionals across the state to have taken part in industrial action in recent months, after more than a year of government negotiations failed to address their concerns about pay and unsafe working conditions.

On 1 October, for the first time in more than 25 years, doctors across Victoria took a four-hour work stoppage. On the steps of state parliament, Australian Salaried Medical Officers Federation (ASMOF) members gathered in the rain, striking for a 30% pay rise over four years, a cap of 12.5 hours on shifts, and a guarantee of three consecutive days off during a fortnight of work.

On the same day, members of the Victorian Allied Health Professionals Association, embroiled in their own – still ongoing – pay dispute with the government, began a 24-hour stop-work action.

The doctors’ strike had come after weeks of localised actions across Melbourne and regional hospitals, but failed to secure a pay deal that members were happy with. A longer strike, scheduled for 21 October, was then cancelled after members narrowly voted to accept a revised 12-month interim offer from the Victorian government.

Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here

In a heated call with about 1,000 doctors days earlier, on 19 October, ASMOF and Australian Medical Association (AMA) executives characterised the offer as “nowhere near close to what we want”, but encouraged doctors to accept the interim deal before government entered caretaker mode ahead of the Victorian election.

It was seen as a capitulation by many doctors, who are frustrated about overwork and understaffing that they say compromises Victoria’s health system. “The conditions for staff and patients in our public hospitals are a problem and won’t be resolved by this deal,” Sarah says.

“The hours we work compromise patient safety,” says a Victorian critical care doctor in training. “It is so unsafe to have one doctor working up to 16 hours a day. You wouldn’t want someone that fatigued flying a plane, or looking after your sick family member.”

Strained public health system

Guardian Australia analysis of dozens of health service annual reports released by the government on 30 October show that in the 2025-26 reporting period, more than 10,000 patients spent over 24 hours in Victorian emergency departments (EDs). Monash Health accounted for the highest number of these patients across its four hospitals (2,501), followed by Albury Wodonga (2,421) and Eastern Health (1,731).

At 16 hospitals, the average ED length of stay for patients who were admitted exceeded 12 hours – a delay that increases the chance of dying in hospital by more than 67%, according to the Australasian College for Emergency Medicine (ACEM).

Patients who are admitted to hospital typically spend twice as long in the ED as those who are discharged home, ACEM has said. “More presentations are requiring hospital admission … yet the number of available hospital beds is decreasing, leading to extended stays in the emergency department.”

Late last month, Ben Carroll announced that a re-elected Labor government would spend $1.5bn to slash emergency wait times by 20%, by expanding EDs at a dozen hospitals and hiring 1,500 workers. But the election pledge was viewed by some as too little, too late for a government seen as accountable for a strained public health system over its 12 years in power.

The Victorian Allied Health Professionals Association criticised the announcement as a “Band-Aid solution” for a “broken healthcare system”.

“Throwing money at ED expansion won’t fix a bed-flow problem that starts with unfilled allied health roles,” it said in a social media post.

Publicly, the AMA and ASMOF welcomed the $1.5bn promise. In a statement, the AMA Victoria president, Dr Simon Judkins, described it as a significant investment, but “only one part of the broader reform needed to fix Victoria’s healthcare system”.

The commitment, though welcome, “does not address access to specialist care or the shortage of available hospital beds, both of which have a major impact on patient flow and the ability of emergency departments to function effectively,” he said.

Privately, frustration is evident. During the 19 October call with doctors, the federal ASMOF president, Dr Roderick McRae, criticised the Victorian government for its treatment of medical professionals, and – according to multiple sources – recommended that instead of voting for Labor, doctors should pay a fine or vote informally.

ASMOF executives subsequently walked back the comments. In a 30 October email apologising to members, it said: “Comments that were of any partisanship [sic] nature were completely inappropriate and ASMOF does not endorse any political party, nor do we wish to influence voter intention.”

Carroll also announced an election pledge to ban violent patients from hospitals for up to 12 months, raising concerns that vulnerable Victorians could be denied healthcare as a result.

Commenting on the policy, Judkins says: “Doctors recognise the growing problem of violence in Victoria’s emergency departments and the urgent need to protect healthcare workers and patients. However, it is equally important that everyone, including people charged with criminal offences, continues to have access to essential healthcare.”

Guardian Australia analysis of the annual reports shows high rates of occupational violence against healthcare workers in 2025–26, up from the previous year. Northern Health logged the most incidents overall – 4,626, at a rate of 73.52 incidents per 100 full-time equivalent staff – followed by Latrobe Regional Health (2,204 incidents, 98.04 per 100 FTE) and Western Health (2,086 incidents, 30.14 per 100 FTE).

Paul Healey, the state secretary of the Health and Community Services Union, says: “There’s a stronger culture of reporting, but the incidents aren’t going down.”

Violent incidents the union’s members report vary from hits, slaps and pushes to more severe. “There’s an example of a staff member who was knocked to the ground, got hit over 20 times to the head, and ended up with facial fractures, [and a] broken collarbone,” Healey says. “There hasn’t been interventions put in place … to make staff feel safe.”

The Liberals, led by Jess Wilson, in August said that if elected they would crack down on escalating violence in hospitals by deploying 70 protective services officers for a two-year pilot at seven major hospitals – but made the announcement without consulting most of the hospitals that would be involved.

“While stronger security measures are welcome, a heavy-handed approach risks escalating situations in a manner that is ultimately detrimental to patient health outcomes and the objectives of medical staff,” Judkins said. “It is preferable that security personnel are appropriately trained.”

A future Liberal government has also pledged to establish SurgerySooner, a $1.27bn plan over four years to halve Victoria’s elective surgery waitlist by giving public patients the choice to undergo surgery at a private hospital. It has also promised $99m for 10 new or expanded patient transit lounges – spaces for patients who are ready to leave hospital but are waiting for discharge arrangements.

‘So much that went wrong’

A coroner’s report published last month on the 2022 death of eight-year-old Amrita Lanka at Monash children’s hospital has outraged doctors, who say the case is emblematic of systemic failures.

The report concluded that the actions of a “relatively junior doctor”, who had been handed over about 18 patients in the ED at the start of the night shift, “caused or contributed to” Lanka’s death from myocarditis, an inflammation of the heart muscle.

It commended Monash Health for an internal review in response to Lanka’s death, which it said “largely obviates the need for formal coronial recommendation”.

A doctor working at Monash Health, who did not wish to be identified, says: “My colleagues are outraged by the lack of findings or recommendations from the coroner regarding Monash Health’s systemic failures.”

“Junior doctors go to work most shifts feeling overworked, under-resourced, and juggling competing priorities that sometimes rely on luck to avoid serious negative outcome. Many of my colleagues feel this could well have been them in the same position.”

Judkins declined to comment on the circumstances of the case, but says AMA Victoria has “serious concerns about the public identification of an individual doctor and, together with ACEM, will raise these concerns directly with the coroner”.

In an email to all Monash Health staff on October 16, its chief executive, Prof Eugine Yafele, said he had contacted the individual doctor to “assure him that he has my full support and confidence”. A Monash spokesperson confirmed that since Lanka’s death, the health service had focused on system-wide issues and improvements to patient care, and was providing support to staff involved.

“It’s so awful what this family has been through,” says the critical care doctor. “There was so much that went wrong that night.”

Junior doctors are often treated as scapegoats and “thrown under the bus in these situations”, he says. “Why is a doctor in training in charge of an emergency department overnight to look after this many patients? How is this considered safe?”

The case, he says, has “brought to light the conditions in which we work and what we’re fighting for. It’s not just about pay – it’s about working conditions, it’s about patient safety.”

*Name has been changed

australia.title: I have noticed a pattern with product ratings that could lead to biased reviews. Is it legal?
australia.snippet: The practice you’ve noticed is colloquially known as ‘review gating’, writes consumer affairs and policy professional Kat George . And no...
australia.content:
I have noticed that when I get an email inviting me to review a product or service I have purchased online or physically, if I select a high rating I am taken to Google to write a review. However, if I select a low rating, I am then told “We are sorry” etc and asked what is wrong. I am not taken to Google to write a review. This would lead to very biased reviews. Is this practice legal? – Tom, Queensland

Kat says: Screening reviews and sorting feedback based on a consumer’s initial sentiment is known colloquially online as “review gating”. It’s a dark pattern that is common enough that Google has banned it outright. And while the Australian consumer law doesn’t name the practice explicitly, it is clearly prohibited under laws relating to business reviews and false and misleading practices.

In early 2026, Google made some pointed changes to its Maps User Generated Content policy. The new policy states that Google does not allow businesses to “discourage or prohibit negative reviews, or selectively solicit positive reviews from customers”. What you have described sounds like businesses doing both of those things.

Google also has real consequences for businesses that are found to be in breach of its policy, so your experience is worth reporting directly to Google. Penalties include removing reviews that breach the policy, placing restrictions and alerts on business profiles, limiting the business’s eligibility to receive new reviews and temporarily hiding historical reviews.

You can report suspicious reviews to Google directly through the Google Map review function, which can be done by clicking the three dots next to a review, then hitting “report review” on the Google Maps website or app. You can also report a business by hitting “suggest an edit” on their Google Maps listing, then selecting “Report business conduct”.

The Australian consumer law also prohibits review gating practices, although not explicitly. Review gating falls under making “false and misleading representations”, which are illegal.

The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission says a business may mislead consumers if it suppresses negative reviews. What you have described certainly sounds like a means of suppressing negative reviews and promoting positive ones.

An example given by the ACCC highlights a 2020 case involving Healthengine, which admitted to not publishing a large volume of negative reviews submitted between 2015 and 2018. It also admitted to editing out negative aspects from published reviews and misrepresenting why ratings weren’t published for some health providers to consumers.

Further, the ACCC has previously reported that 37% of online businesses (in a sweep of 130) were manipulating online reviews. These businesses were found to have created fake positive reviews for themselves, or scrubbed negative reviews.

Given the ACCC’s interest in this issue, it’s also worth reporting businesses there as well, which you can do via the online form on its website. While the ACCC won’t take action in your individual matter, if multiple reports are made about the same issue or business it may be able to identify a systemic issue warranting action.

Ultimately, the practice you have described is clearly illegal, so it’s well worth making it known to Google and the regulator.

australia.title: Australians are streaming more music than ever – but homegrown songs are being skipped
australia.snippet: Annual review of the streaming market shows discord between Australian listeners and local music Get our weekend culture and lifestyle em...
australia.content:
Australian musicians are headlining stages all over the world – and Australians are streaming more music than ever before. Yet an annual review from Apra Amcos shows a lack of harmony between Australia’s online music listeners and its homegrown tunes.

In its yearly review released ahead of Australian music month, Apra Amcos, the organisation that represents Australian songwriters, reported the local market saw approximately 640m more music streams in 2026 than in 2025. In that same period, the proportion of Australian songs that were streamed suffered its largest annual fall in four years – from 9.5% in 2025 to 8.5% in 2026. The reality offline is no better, with the report finding there are now 182 live music venues in Australia per million citizens – down from 206 venues per million citizens in 2018.

The pattern isn’t only in what we consume, but in what we create. User-generated content (UGC), when platform users upload their own videos accompanied by a band or artist’s song, is a market that has grown by 28% in the past 12 months, totalling 746.2bn streams – yet the amount of UGC featuring Australian songs has nearly halved.

It’s not all doom and gloom: Apra Amcos is calling for minimum local music requirements for streaming platforms, similar to those of commercial and community radio stations, with levies for the platforms that don’t comply. It is also lobbying for a federal tax rebate for live music – to the tune of 30% – to help cover expenditure incurred by venues and artists when staging live music. Tasmania is leading the charge, becoming the first state to trial such a rebate.

  • Are there any Australian artists or bands you think people should be listening to more? Share your tips in the comments

australia.title: Surf’s up, lights up: floodlight-lit night surfing could be coming to the Gold Coast – but could it bring unwanted fins?
australia.snippet: Lighting up Snapper Rocks by night could help with overcrowding, but some fear permanent floodlights could attract sharks or turn their c...
australia.content:
As the sun sets on one of the world’s most iconic breaks, thousands of surfers paddle into one last wave, exit the water and disappear into the bright lights of the Gold Coast. But that could change after the city council this week endorsed plans to floodlight Snapper Rocks – a famous rocky outcrop and world-class right-hand point break, located at the southern end of Rainbow Bay – for night surfing.

The $100,000 temporary trial would be part of the 2027 World Surf League championship tour event held at Coolangatta, the southernmost suburb of the Australian coastal city.

The plan has raised concerns that more regular use of floodlights on the water could attract sharks – and risks transforming a place of natural beauty into a theme park.

A local surfing identity, Andrew “Andy Mac” McKinnon, says night surfing at Snapper would be “a great spectacle” for special events such as the WSL, or the Olympics. Framed on two sides by rocks that cut into the ocean and by the Rainbow Bay surf club and Snapper Rocks road on another, McKinnon says the point break is the “ideal bay to light up”.

“Snapper’s absolutely perfect,” he says. “It is one of the greatest surfing amphitheatres, a natural amphitheatre. To add night surfing to it would be so dynamic – I think everyone will be pretty excited about this.”

McKinnon led efforts to create the Gold Coast World Surfing Reserve in 2016 and continues to preside over the nonprofit committee dedicated to protecting this 16km stretch coast from Burleigh Heads to Snapper a decade later. A champion surfer in his own right, Andy Mac’s storied career saw him surf with Coolangatta mates who would become some of the sport’s global legends including the first WSL world champion, Peter “PT” Townend, and fellow WSL champ Wayne “Rabbit” Bartholomew.

The 73-year-old is no stranger to night surfing, both as a participant and as an organiser. In 1971, McKinnon surfed under “Hollywood-style” floodlights at Hawaii’s famous Mākaha beach, while in 1988 he took on the legendary left handers of New Zealand’s Manu bay at night. McKinnon recalls both as unnerving experiences.

“There were times you’d be totally blinded by the floodlights, and then there were times when you weren’t under the lights and you’d be in total darkness out there,” he says. “It was pretty spooky.”

Describing the latter scenario as “surfing by braille”, McKinnon says it was harder to catch waves under the lights of those pioneering events than by the light of a full moon – which he has done a couple of times for pleasure, rather than for competition’s sake.

McKinnon also helped organise the first light night surfing in Queensland at the Gold Coast’s Surfers Paradise in 1996, an event he recalls as “a pretty wild time”.

“There were these electrical storms going off out on the horizon,” he says. “The city chief lifeguard at the time, Warren Young, was sitting right alongside me and with the storm, the lights and the surfers out in the water … we were both having kittens.”

But while McKinnon is otherwise pretty relaxed about the idea of entering the ocean at night, he believes lighting it up seven days a week could be “inviting trouble”. He is not alone. News of the night surfing plan drew hundreds of comments online with one key theme circling them: sharks.

Councillor Donna Gates raised that concern at the transport and infrastructure committee meeting on 2 November, asking if it was “an old wives’ tale” that sharks were “more prevalent at dusk or evening”.

A city officer responded by saying staff found no evidence to suggest that “surfing at night carries any increased risk of shark attack than any other time of the day”.

Dr Vincent Raoult, a Griffith University shark expert, says however that – when it comes to one of the state’s most infamous shark species, at least – Gates was not peddling in folklore.

“After sunset and into the night coincides with the time where bull sharks, in particular, are most active,” Raoult says. “So there’s a bit of a heightened risk there.”

Raoult, who is a senior lecturer in environmental sustainability and management, says Snapper Rocks is near the Tweed River. “We already know that areas around river mouths are at risk of heightened bull shark activity and greater risk to swimmers and surfers – and [night surfing] would just increase those risks,” he says.

Raoult says a one-off night surfing event “sounds like a cool experience” and, if well planned, could have negligible impacts on the environment. But the light pollution of more regular use could cause significant environmental impacts, including attracting bait fish and squid which would, in turn, attract predators such as sharks.

“Sharks are really good at learning and learning patterns,” Raoult says. “So if they do start to get exposed to a pattern where, if they come to this beach that’s lit up like a Christmas tree and there’s a bunch of food that’s available, then they’ll actually learn to visit that spot for an easy feed.”

Council’s report identifies “overcrowding of surf breaks” as a challenge for “one of the world’s great surfing cities”, noting the number of “annual surf craft riders” increased from 1.1 million to 3.2 million over the decade to 2025. Night surfing is flagged as means of accommodating the ever-increasing number of surfers, and the proposed WSL event was pitched as a trial to provide “an evidence base” for more of it.

These overcrowded breaks have already led to a community of surfers who paddle out on to Gold Coast waves after dark, says Harry Gordon, from Surfrider Foundation Australia’s Gold Coast and Tweed branch.

“On a decent swell, you could go to Snapper and you’ll see 50 or 60 people surfing in the middle of the night – if the moon’s right,” Gordon says. “People night surf. That’s OK. But do you need lights to do it?”

Gordon says that, as a “one-off spectacle”, night surfing seems a reasonable proposal. But “longer-term trials or a permanent initiative” was “a very different proposition” – one that he says would require “significant assessment and consultation well beyond what is proposed in this trial”.

“We’re open to all options to reduce overcrowding and enable people to have a healthy lifestyle and to surf,” he says. “But that can’t be at the cost of the environmental values of our area.”

The passionate bodysurfer and boardrider acknowledges that the Gold Coast relies heavily upon tourism, but says the city is not, in of itself, “a theme park”.

“It’s a place where people live and it’s our community,” Gordon says. “So while attractions are good, we don’t need to turn our whole lifestyle and our community into a tourism attraction.”

A city spokesperson says its Surfing Infrastructure Masterplan (SIM) has undertaken investigations “into the potential ecological and safety impacts of using artificial lighting for ocean recreation after dark”.

This work included a risk assessment that considered shark interactions and identified a range of mitigation measures, including “limiting the use of lighting to specific periods and not operating after heavy rainfall”, the spokesperson says.

“It should also be noted that the underlying risk of shark attack in Australia is extremely low and the city is focused on managing a range of risks that might be introduced through lighting of a surf break.”

The night surfing event proposal must still be issued permits by the city.

world.title: Lewis Hamilton visits Egypt’s Rafah crossing and Gaza aid facilities
world.snippet: Seven-time F1 world champion tours border area and logistics warehouses operated by Egyptian Red Crescent Lewis Hamilton has visited Egyp...
world.content:
Lewis Hamilton has visited Egypt’s Rafah border crossing with the Gaza Strip to meet organisations sending humanitarian aid to the territory.

The seven-time Formula 1 world champion has spoken out about conflict and humanitarian crises in the region, and has called for peace. He has frequently posted on social media about children killed in Israeli airstrikes in Gaza and called for a ceasefire.

“I think we need to make sure we’re pushing to free Congo, free Sudan, free Syria, free Palestine. I think there’s a lot of peace that I’m hoping we get to at some stage,” Hamilton said last month.

A ceasefire agreement reached last year has halted major combat operations in Gaza, but the amount of aid getting in to the strip continues to fall far short of the agreed-upon minimum of 600 trucks a day.

Israeli forces have continued to advance, expanding their control from 53% of the territory to at least 60%, an independent commission of UN experts said last month.

Airstrikes also continue across, and Israeli fire along the advancing front has killed at least 196 Palestinians, including 18 women, 32 boys and 11 girls, the commission said.

Hamilton toured Egypt’s Rafah border crossing with Gaza before visiting logistics warehouses operated by the Egyptian Red Crescent, which facilitates the entry of aid in to Gaza.

At the crossing, Hamilton greeted aid workers with “Assalamu alaikum” a widely used Arabic greeting meaning “peace be upon you.” He shook hands and briefly spoke to workers and officials.

Khaled Megawer, the governor of North Sinai, where Rafah is located, said the visit was intended to help Hamilton learn about Egypt’s efforts to send aid to Gaza.

The visit comes after Hamilton made his 400th race start on Sunday at the Sao Paulo Grand Prix at Interlagos.

The first black F1 driver, he made his debut with McLaren in 2007. He is only the second F1 driver to start 400 races after his former teammate Fernando Alonso, who achieved the milestone in 2024.

world.title: Collision of two trains in Egypt kills at least seven
world.snippet: President orders prompt investigation after one train derails in collision in al-Ayyat about 50km from Cairo Seven people were killed and...
world.content:
Seven people were killed and at least 125 injured when two trains collided on Sunday south of the Egyptian capital, Cairo, officials said.

The crash occurred in al-Ayyat district in Giza province, about 50km (30 miles) south of Cairo, when a train travelling to Fayoum province crashed into the rear of a train heading to the southern province of Aswan, according to the transport ministry.

An inspection indicated that the Cairo-Aswan train had been stationary on the same track, officials said.

The health ministry gave the casualty toll, adding more than 70 of the injured were discharged after receiving treatment.

Train derailments and crashes are common in Egypt, where the railway system has a history of mismanagement and poor maintenance of equipment. In recent years the government has announced modernisation initiatives to improve its railways.

Ayman Gamal, a resident of Kafr Girza in al-Ayyat where the crash occurred, said people rushed to the scene, pulled out survivors and called ambulances.

Gamal said he saw about 80 of the injured being taken by ambulances to hospital. Some passengers were trapped inside one of the carriages of the stationary train and died, he said.

Egypt’s president, Abdel Fatah al-Sisi, said in a social media post that he had ordered a prompt investigation.

Outside al-Wasta central hospital in Beni Suef province, where some of the injured were taken for treatment, survivors said passengers were in shock and struggling to breathe because of all the dust that was kicked up. Nearby villagers eventually got them out, they said.

Farha Gamal, a survivor who was inside the Fayyoum train, said she saw some of the passengers who appeared dead and others were struggling to find their way out of the car. “There were other cars that were completely mangled,” she said in an interview.

Emergency teams and cranes were dispatched to the crash site to clear the wreckage and restore train services to their normal schedule as soon as possible, the Egyptian railway authority said.

Last September, a train driver and his assistant were injured after two freight trains collided in the same district.

Egypt’s deadliest train crash was in 2002 when more than 300 people were killed after a fire broke out on an overnight train journeying from Cairo to southern Egypt.

world.title: How African philosophies inspired a new approach to staging film festivals in Manchester
world.snippet: See My World, an event highlighting the pan-African thought via film, poetry and dance, builds on momentum sparked by local activists and...
world.content:
African philosophies including exploring how lessons from the past can shape the present and near future have inspired a film festival coming to Manchester.

See My World, a day dedicated to independent creators from across the African diaspora in the north of England, will take place at the Contact theatre on 21 November.

The festival is part of See My World’s year-round programme showcasing pan-African arts, culture and events.

It reflects the determination among creatives and activists in Manchester to build on the legacy of the 1945 Pan-African Congress in Manchester – which connected luminaries of postwar independence movements with a shared vision of liberation – after last year’s 80th anniversary commemorations.

See My World’s CEO and artistic director, Tunde Adekoya, said this month’s film festival was taking inspiration from across the spectrum of pan-African thought, including the works of Kenyan writers John Mbiti, an Anglican theologian who died in 2019, and Ngũgĩ wa Thiong’o, the author of the groundbreaking 1986 book Decolonising the Mind who died last year.

Both writers rejected the colonial conceit that African thought was inferior, stressed the importance of community and saw reclaiming African ways of knowing as essential to a people’s self-understanding.

While Mbiti sought common ground between African religions and Christianity, Ngũgĩ was a Marxist. He argued colonialism was motivated by cultural and economic conquest, and that European powers used language as their sharpest instrument. Ngũgĩ famously abandoned English to write in Gikuyu, a Bantu language mainly spoken in Kenya and criticised the role missionary Christianity played in colonial rule.

Adekoya said: “It’s a day dedicated to pan-African and global majority films from the north of England with exclusive premieres of documentaries we’ve been working on, which weave together expressions of liberation through art forms like poetry and dance.

“The whole idea is that it’s like a playground in search of strategies of liberation, using the festival as a way to explore different philosophies.

“John Mbiti explores the philosophy and spiritual understandings of time through the concept of Sasa na Zamani – in which the past informs everything that happens moving forward. That reflects how we constantly go back to pan-African histories to inform how we progress.”

Film-makers have been invited to submit films lasting up to 30 minutes from across genres, with no screening fees charged.

As well as submissions, the festival will feature documentaries produced by See My World. They include Homage, a “cinematic love letter to dance” that traces a culture through present-day portraits illustrating dance artists and archival material from Manchester, telling a story of joy, loss, migration, rhythm and resistance. Meanwhile, Poetic Justice explores how pan-African thought and Manchester’s poetry scene speak across decades.

Adekoya added: “The idea is that we would go against the norm of how film festivals are, because when we think about decolonisation, we think about how structures have been created to alienate and exclude communities.

“So we thought our film festival would look more at how we make film accessible and how stories that deserve to be seen get seen. Throughout the day we will have different activities, from exhibitions to explorations of our performances, discussions, Q&As, insights into directors’ processes, and workshops.

“We’ve been looking for literature and concepts that inform us and give us an understanding of who we truly are. And as works from thinkers like John Mbiti have come into our sphere, they have really emboldened us to think differently about our place in the world and what we do.”

See My World film festival runs from 2pm to 11pm on Saturday 21 November at Contact theatre, Oxford Road, Manchester.

world.title: Kenyan doomsday sect leader jailed for 200 years for murder of 190 children
world.snippet: Paul Mackenzie convicted over deaths of children and one adult after followers were ordered to starve themselves and their families The l...
world.content:
The leader of a Kenyan doomsday sect has been sentenced to 200 years in prison for the murders of 190 children and one adult in one of the world’s worst cult disasters in recent history.

The sentence, comprising 100 years for murder by starvation and 100 years by direct homicide, came two weeks after the court in Kenya’s coastal city of Mombasa found the cult leader guilty of the crimes.

Prosecutors said Paul Mackenzie and his Good News International church ran ​a Christian doomsday sect whose members were ordered to starve themselves and their children to death to go to heaven before the world ended.

His accomplices threatened and beat victims to ensure they followed his orders. The emaciated bodies were found scattered in shallow graves and dumped in latrines. Some had been buried alive.

Mackenzie was arrested in 2023 after police received a tipoff, and weeks later authorities began uncovering bodies in shallow graves in the Shakahola forest near the coast in south-eastern Kenya.

In total, more than 400 bodies have been recovered. Many were severely decomposed and only 26 could be identified.

Mackenzie denied murder charges, saying he did not force the victims to starve, but the court rejected that argument.

The Shakahola tragedy has gripped Kenya since the discovery of mass graves in the forest more than three years ago.

It raised questions about how Mackenzie was able to continue operating despite being on the radar of the authorities since 2017, when police searched his premises.

In 2019, authorities shut down Mackenzie’s church and he relocated ‌to the Shakahola forest, police said.

The case has also led to calls for tougher oversight of churches and other religious organisations in a country where religious faith plays a prominent role in public life.

Mackenzie, a former taxi driver, forbade cult members from sending their children to school and from going to hospital when they were ill, describing such institutions as satanic.

Cult members lived in makeshift homes of polythene sheeting and thatch that Mackenzie divided into areas with biblical names such as Jerusalem and Judea.

The plight of his followers began ​to emerge in March 2023, when a man told ​police his brother and wife had starved their children ​to death in the forest on Mackenzie’s orders.

Mackenzie was arrested but released on bail, after which relatives said he brought forward the date ​on which he told his followers the ‌world would end. Police rearrested him and ​started combing through the forest more systematically and began exhuming mass graves.

Last month’s judgment covered 191 deaths while investigations into more than 200 other deaths are continuing.

Justice Diana Kavedza-Mochache said in a hearing lasting more than eight hours that in some cases children were isolated and denied food while their parents watched.

Mackenzie faces other charges over the forest deaths, including those of terrorism, which he has denied.

Prosecutors said that while he was in detention he also directed the deaths of 52 people in Kwa Binzaro village, about 18 miles from Shakahola. Mackenzie has pleaded not guilty in that case.

Reuters contributed reporting

world.title: ANC faces bruising defeat in South African local elections with 80% of ballots counted
world.snippet: Former liberation movement’s share of national vote almost 14 percentage points below 2021 result The African National Congress is on cou...
world.content:
The African National Congress is on course to suffer a bruising defeat in South Africa’s local elections, with the once dominant party of Nelson Mandela falling to under a third of the vote nationally with more than 80% of ballots counted.

Wednesday’s fragmented vote marks another stage in the decline of the ANC, which has led national governments since the end of white minority apartheid rule in 1994. High unemployment, crime, corruption and poor local service delivery have all contributed to voters turning away from the party.

The former liberation movement is projected to lose its status as the biggest party in the two most populous provinces, Gauteng and KwaZulu-Natal, as parties began coalition negotiations behind closed doors. The final results are expected to be announced on Sunday.

The ANC was on 31.8% of the vote nationally, almost 14 percentage points below its 2021 local election result. The centre-right, white-led Democratic Alliance (DA) had 24.1% of the vote, while the uMkhonto weSizwe (MK) party of the former ANC president Jacob Zuma was on 9.3%.

Turnout also rose in Wednesday’s poll. The election commission estimated that 54.5% of registered voters cast their ballot, up from 46% five years ago.

The final shape of coalitions in some of the country’s biggest cities remained unclear with the final votes still being counted. Senior figures in key parties said they would talk with almost anyone, while keeping negotiating strategies under wraps.

In Johannesburg, South Africa’s commercial capital and biggest city, with 4.8 million people, voters have had to contend with regular water and power cuts, uncollected rubbish and potholes. The municipality, which has seen 10 changes of mayor in the last decade amid unstable coalitions, has admitted to a 220bn rand (£9.9bn) infrastructure spending backlog.

With just over half of votes counted in Johannesburg, the DA was leading with 40%, having run an energetic campaign under Helen Zille, a 75-year-old former Cape Town mayor. The ANC, which leads the current coalition, was in second place on 17.5%. ActionSA, a rightwing party led by Herman Mashaba, was on 15.5%. Mashaba has pledged never to work with Zille, whom he calls “racist”, something she vehemently denies.

Many of the ANC’s township strongholds have yet to report full results. The Council for Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR), a respected thinktank, has projected the DA will finish with 34%, the ANC 20% and ActionSA 16.8%.

Coalitions in Gauteng’s three city municipalities are often negotiated together. The DA is leading in all three.

The MK party, led by 84-year-old Zuma as he continues to weather and deny numerous corruption allegations, is expected to displace the ANC as the largest party in KwaZulu-Natal. Founded in 2023, it mixes socially conservative Zulu nationalism with pledges to redistribute land and wealth from white to black South Africans.

With half of votes counted in eThekwini municipality, which contains Durban, the MK had 41%, meaning other parties could form a coalition to keep it out of power. Meanwhile, the DA is projected to maintain its majority in Cape Town, despite growing middle-class anger over rising housing costs.

Voters choose a local councillor and a party, with seats allocated via proportional representation. Councillors will then have two weeks to elect mayors and form municipal governments.
